newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire warns Rwanda, U.N. to appoint envoy to region.
newsitem.headline: Zaire warns Rwanda, U.N. to appoint envoy to region.

text.p: Zaire warned Rwanda it would fight to defend its territory and its vast mineral wealth after the two sides fought a mortar battle across their border.

For the first time since ethnic warfare erupted in eastern Zaire two weeks ago, Zairean and Rwandan soldiers on Tuesday exchanged sustained fire across the river that divides the two countries, fuelling the chaos that has driven half a million Rwandan and Burundian refugees from border camps inside Zaire.
In New York U.N. sources said the United Nations was set to appoint Canada's ambassador to Washington as its new representative to deal with the crisis in eastern Zaire.

But the envoy, Raymond Chretien, nephew of Canada's prime minister, Jean Chretien, will only serve for a month as an interim representative until a more permanent mission can be established. He leaves for the region on November 6.

Fighting between Zairean troops and ethnic Tutsis, who first settled in what is now eastern Zaire some 200 years ago, threatens to draw in the Tutsi-dominated armies of Zaire's small neighbours Rwanda and Burundi.
Both deny Zairean accusations they back the Tutsi rebels, known as Banyamulenge, who have taken the town of Uvira and threaten to overrun the South Kivu provincial capital of Bukavu.

Reuters reporters and other witnesses in the Rwandan border town of Cyangugu, just across the border from Bukavu, spoke of exchanges lasting about two hours. Aid workers at one stage had to take refuge from the firing, they said.
"It was a fairly sustained bombardment," Reuters Television producer Tony Wende said. "The Rwandans fired mortars, anti-aircraft guns and heavy machineguns with tracers."
Zairean Foreign Minister Kitidwa Tumansi appeared on state television after the fighting to repeat Zaire's charges against Rwanda of territorial ambition.
"Zaire warns those who think the time has come to carve out new political and economic entities with hegemonic designs on its precious and strategic materials," Kitidwa said.
"If Rwanda persists in this dream it will be responsible for what happens in the Great Lakes sub-region," he added.
Zaire is rich in strategic minerals that virtually guaranteed Western support for its corrupt and inept government led by President Mobutu Sese Seko during the Cold War years.
At the weekend Mobutu, having treatment for cancer in Switzerland, sought to reassert his authority in Zaire's eastern borderlands by placing the two troubled Kivu provinces under military rule.
The fighting has created the most serious refugee crisis in Africa since apocalyptic massacres and civil war in Rwanda in 1994 sent two million people fleeing into nearby states.

Most of the latest refugees on the move are Rwandan Hutus. Some are former soldiers and militiamen and many took part in the 1994 massacre of up to a million minority Tutsis and their sympathisers in Rwanda before Tutsi rebels drove them out.
The refugees fear reprisals in Rwanda but some have headed back home anyway, preferring that risk to violence in Zaire.
The refugee agency UNHCR says nearly half a million refugees have packed a tent camp on volcanic rock outside the eastern Zaire city of Goma, to the north of Bukavu.
The agency says it has no access to up to 400,000 Rwandan Hutus around Goma and 300,000 in Uvira and Goma. It appealed to countries to provide satellite photos to help track them.
In Brussels, the European Union's aid commissioner Emma Bonino said one million people, many of them already refugees from Rwanda and Burundi, could die in Zaire.
She accused the world of standing aloof from the tragedy.
European diplomats and officials from major humanitarian agencies began urgent talks in Geneva late on Tuesday over the unfolding crisis in eastern Zaire, diplomats said.
The closed-door meeting, chaired by French Secretary of State for Emergency Humanitarian Action Xavier Emmanuelli, was to examine how to meet the survival needs of the homeless.
